title: Winds and the Witch of the Deep Cave
subtitle: Book Four of the Castle Everstair stories
refrain: But nobody picks how they started.
styleString: Painterly children's storybook illustration, soft watercolor and colored-pencil texture, visible brushwork, warm golden lamplight against deep indigo night, lavender and pearl-grey stone, generous sparkle and stardust trails, big expressive eyes, gentle rounded shapes, no harsh lines, no photorealism, no text in image.

characters.name: Winds
characters.sheet: Winds: young jaguar cub the same size and age as Cottontail; pale grey-blue coat with cloud-white rosette spots, a tuft of bright wavy blue hair exactly the shape of Cottontail's pink tuft, very wide-open sky-blue eyes, a huge cheerful grin; sturdy ordinary paws; no wings, no mermaid tail, no magic, no sparkle; a woven pale-blue grass bracelet on one front leg.

characters.name: Baby Jag Cottontail
characters.sheet: Baby Jag Cottontail: young jaguar cub, soft yellow-gold coat with black rosette spots, a tuft of bright pink wavy hair, warm amber eyes, sturdy ordinary paws with small curved claws; no wings and no mermaid tail; a woven seashell bracelet on one front leg.

characters.name: Princess Moon
characters.sheet: Princess Moon: young girl, long wavy pink hair, large dark-blue eyes, rosy cheeks; delicate translucent golden fairy wings with fine filigree veining; silver iridescent mermaid tail with pearl-sheen scales; small gold crown topped with a crescent moon; pearl necklace with a gold crescent pendant.

characters.name: Baby Lady
characters.sheet: Baby Lady: small fluffy cocker-spaniel puppy, golden-cream curly ears, dark round eyes; iridescent pearl-white fairy wings, smaller and softer than Moon's; pale silver-pink mermaid tail in place of back legs — she has no back legs and no back paws, her puppy body ends in the mermaid tail, front paws only; tiny gold crescent charm on a pearl collar.

characters.name: Elysian
characters.sheet: Elysian: very old witch, one hundred and five years old, small and hunched like a hook; deeply wrinkled pale grey-lavender face with a long nose and heavy-lidded eyes; floor-length black hair that, when light shines through it, drapes into the unmistakable shape of a skull — two round sockets, a jaw, a grin — made only of falling hair, never a real skull, and it shifts when she moves; plain ragged high-collared black robe; carries a thin black wand; her cave holds a round black cauldron glowing sick green, a worn twig broom, and an enormous open spell book; no pet and no helper; ugly-scary but calm and certain, never gleeful, never gory or horrific.

characters.name: Evilest
characters.sheet: Evilest: pale girl, black hair, tall spiky black crown, high-collared black gown, arms crossed, sharp confident smile.

characters.name: Cheeblest
characters.sheet: Cheeblest: pale girl, black hair in two bows and pigtails, deep-purple dress, watchful rather than cruel, eyes slightly too soft for the tower.

characters.name: Beedlist
characters.sheet: Beedlist: pale girl dressed entirely in black: long straight black hair, plain long black high-collared dress, black shoes, black ribbon; no crown; no color anywhere on her; small calm unreadable face; perfectly still posture, hands folded in front of her.

cover.imagePrompt: Book cover composition: the grey-blue sky jaguar cub sliding down a visible ribbon of wind out of tall moonlit clouds, grinning hugely, about to bump foreheads with the pink-haired jaguar cub who stands braced and delighted on the bottom steps of the great glowing castle stair where it meets the sea — and beneath that bottom step, a thin dark seam in the stone leaks a faint sick-green glow that neither of them has noticed. Moon flying small and joyful behind them. Perfectly round full moon (never a crescent). Open sky in the upper third for the title. No rabbits, no other animals.

questions: Elysian never yelled and never cackled. She was calm, and kind-sounding, and completely sure — and completely wrong. Can somebody be wrong even when they are very, very sure? How can you tell the difference between being sure and being right?
Moon and Baby Lady never argued for three whole books — and their silly argument in the rain was the happiest moment in this one. Why can a little argument be a sign that everything is safe?
Winds and Cottontail have no magic at all, and that is exactly what saved everyone. What can you do that isn't magic, but is all yours?

Moon offered Elysian the plain rain, and she wouldn't stand in it — because letting the old mix-up wash away would mean it really was a mistake, and not a finishing. Why do you think that is so hard, even for grownups? Do you think she will ever stand in the rain?
lookAndFind: There's a crescent moon hiding in almost every picture — even down in the deep cave, where the moon can't reach. Can you find them all? And whenever you see Elysian, look closely at her long black hair: can you spot the skull hiding in it before it moves?

spreads.title: Under the bottom step
spreads.text:
The stair goes up. You know about up.
You've climbed it with princess and jaguar and pup,
past the gap near the ninety-ninth bend (you hop over),
past the clouds, past the wind, past the last bit of blue.

But here is a question three books never asked
(and questions, like puddles, can hide something vast):
what's under the bottom step? Under. Below.
Nobody wondered. Not once. Would you know?

For under the bottom step, deeper than deep,
lower down than the dark where the sea goes to sleep,
there's a cave. And it's old. And it's quiet. And listen:
it's been there this whole entire time.
spreads.imagePrompt: Wide establishing shot, vertical drama: the grand glowing spiral stair rising from the moonlit sea toward the lavender castle and an enormous perfectly round full moon (never a crescent) — but the weight of the image is at the bottom, where beneath the water line, revealed like a storybook cutaway through rock, a vast hidden cave of wet black stone sits directly under the stair's first step, utterly dark except for one tiny far-off sick-green glow. No characters. Awe, scale, and a held-breath secret; gentle, not frightening.

vocab.definition: a big hollow room inside the rock, down under the ground

spreads.title: The yes-dear autumn
spreads.text:
That autumn the grownups went quiet. All through.
The cook. The lamplighter. The guard-captain too.
They smiled and they nodded, and all that they said
was "Yes, dear." "That's fine, dear." "Of course." "Go ahead."

Nobody shooed anyone out of the kitchen.
Nobody grumped about sand on the floor.
Nobody hollered out "Careful!" or "DON'T!"
They didn't say don't anymore.

And the kids saw it first, and the kids saw it only.
(You can't tell a grownup a grownup's gone wrong
when all that the grownup will answer is "Yes, dear.")
Something was missing. Something was gone.
spreads.imagePrompt: Warm castle kitchen interior at evening: a plump cook, a thin lamplighter and a round guard-captain all wearing the exact same small calm smile, standing oddly still and looking pleasantly at nothing; in the foreground Moon and Baby Lady exchange a worried glance with each other. Cozy golden lamplight, steam and copper pots, and something faintly wrong in the stillness. Unsettling but gentle.

vocab.definition: a person whose job is lighting all the lamps
complained in a growly, grouchy way

spreads.title: The word in the book
spreads.text:
They sent for the sisters. All three of them came.
And Evilest tested the grownups. She stomped.
She hollered. She tracked in the mud of the shore.
"Yes, dear," said the grownups. "That's fine, dear." "Of course."

(And here's a strange thing that she found on the way:
when nobody stops you, it's lonely to play.)

Then Cheeblest spoke up, and her voice was all small:
"When I was quite little, I heard the word aunt.
I asked who she was. Just the once. That was all.
And they went very still, and said, Don't. And I didn't.
But I can't stop remembering how they said don't —
like the word was a door they were leaning against."

And Beedlist said nothing, the way that she does.
But she opened her book, and she wrote one small word,
and she did a thing Beedlist has never once done:
she showed them the page.

And the word was: BELOW.
spreads.imagePrompt: Lamplit castle hall at night: Evilest mid-stomp in muddy boots being answered by a serenely smiling guard who should be scolding her; Cheeblest standing small, hugging her own arms, speaking; and at the center Beedlist holding up her small black book, open to one page bearing tiny unreadable pen marks, while Moon and Baby Lady lean in to look. Warm gold lamplight against deep indigo shadow, worried small faces.

vocab.definition: your mom or dad's sister

spreads.title: Winds
spreads.text:
"If we're going below," said the cat with pink hair,
"then we need my best friend. He's the finder of air."
And she climbed the tall rock where the seabirds all sit,
and she whistled a whistle with wind inside it.

And down through the clouds, on a slide made of breeze,
came a jaguar the grey-blue of faraway seas,
with rosettes like clouds and a tuft of blue hair
(the same as her pink one — the sky's version — there),

and he hollered the whole way down: "COTTONTAIL!"
and she hollered up "WINDS!" and they bonked heads. Twice.
She sails on the water. He sails on the air.
Since always, they've met at the one place they share:

the horizon — that line, thin as thread, far from land,
where the sea and the sky lean their heads on each other —
the only place both of them ever can stand.
He's loud where she's dry. He's a friend like a brother.

And Winds has no magic. No shine. Not a drop.
What Winds has: a nose that can always smell OUT.
You can bury that jaguar. Blindfold him. Spin him.
Wherever the out is, the out is deep in him.
spreads.imagePrompt: Bright windy morning over the sea: the grey-blue sky jaguar cub sliding down a long visible ribbon of breeze from tall sunlit clouds, mid-holler with joy, while the pink-haired jaguar cub stands on a tall empty seabird rock whistling up at him, pink hair blown sideways; behind them the horizon line bright and thin where sea and sky meet. Sparkling spray, wind-blown fur, pure delight. No rabbits, no birds, no other animals.

vocab.definition: the flower-shaped spots on a jaguar's coat
a cloth tied over your eyes so you can't peek

spreads.title: The down-stair
spreads.text:
Four girls and a pup and two jaguars went down
to the very first step, where the seafoam goes round,
and Winds put his nose to the seam of the stone,
and everyone hushed.

"There's air under this one," he said. "Moving air.
Old air. But moving. There's a somewhere down there."
So Cottontail hooked in one claw, like a key,
and the bottom step opened.

It swung like the lid of a chest, and beneath it: stairs.
A down-stair. A dark one. Steep, narrow, and old,
with no moon and no sea and no silver and gold,
and away at the bottom, a little green glow,
a green that no garden would ever let grow.

The children held hands, and the jaguars went first.
Some stairs you go up. This was one in reverse.
spreads.imagePrompt: At the foot of the great glowing stair where it meets the seafoam: the bottom step swung open like the lid of a chest, revealing narrow stone stairs descending into blackness with a faint sick-green glow far below; the blue-haired sky jaguar sniffing at the dark opening, the pink-haired jaguar cub with one claw still hooked under the step's edge, and behind them the four pale girls and the small winged puppy holding hands in a chain, all lit warm gold by moonlight. Perfectly round full moon (never a crescent). Courage and wonder, not terror.

vocab.definition: the backwards way — down instead of up

spreads.title: Elysian
spreads.text:
The down-stair went down for a very long time,
and ended at last in a cave like a hall:
a cauldron, mid-bubble, all green in the black;
a broom, standing patient; a wand by the wall;
a spell book, spread open to spells.

And her.

She was bent like a hook. She was hundred-and-five.
No cat and no crow and no helper. No friend.
Just her and her four things, alone in the dark,
for years upon years upon years, with no end —
and here is the sad part: she'd never once noticed.

Her voice, when it came, came out deep and came slow,
like it had a long way to climb up from below.
And her hair — her long hair — was as black as the pot,
and when the green light came through it, it fell
in a shape that hair shouldn't:
two sockets. A jaw. A grin, made of hair.
Not a real skull. It's only the way that it falls.
But it moved when she moved.
Which is worse.

"Hello," said the witch, and the cave said it after.
"I am your aunt Elysian. Family. True —
from the side of the family nobody speaks of.
Come closer. You look so unfinished. Come through."
spreads.imagePrompt: Deep beneath the castle: a vast cave hall of wet black stone lit by the strong sick-green glow of a bubbling cauldron that keeps the whole scene clearly visible — beside it a worn twig broom standing against the wall, a thin black wand, and an enormous open spell book on a stone ledge; at the cauldron the ancient hunched witch stirs slowly, her floor-length black hair catching the green light so it drapes into the clear shape of a skull — two sockets, a jaw, a grin made only of hair; at the far cave mouth, the children tiny and huddled in the glowing stair doorway. Bone-white highlights on wet stone; unsettling but gentle, never gory.

vocab.definition: a witch's big round cooking pot

spreads.title: The Zapping
spreads.text:
"The Zapping," she said, "is a beautiful thing."
(She stirred as she spoke. She was smiling. It's worse
when they smile.) "Ink and shadow and water, all mixed
in a basin. You're dipped. And you rise. And you're finished.
Complete. Not a thing left to fix or to chase.
It happened to me when I was in college,
and ever since then, I've been done. I've been through.
And everyone else is so sadly unfinished.
I zap whom I can. It's a kindness I do."

But here's what is true, and she never was told:
on the day of her Zapping, a long time ago,
somebody filling her basin picked wrong —
two jars on a shelf, and a hand in a hurry.
Not wicked. Just wrong, the way socks can be wrong.
Nobody noticed. Nobody said.

And some part of Elysian stopped at that basin,
and stood there, and waited, and eighty years passed,
and the rest of her aged, and the stopped part just stood there.
She thinks she was finished.
She froze.
spreads.imagePrompt: Dream-memory vision with soft dissolving edges, in faded sepia-lavender tones, framed by curling green cauldron steam: a candlelit stone hall of a college long ago, a young woman in simple ceremonial robes stepping down into a wide stone basin of dark water, gowned attendants pouring gracefully from two tall jars — and one of the jars, subtly, is the wrong one, its liquid a shade too dark, and nobody in the picture has noticed. Tender, sad, softly lit; the young woman's face hopeful, nothing frightening.

vocab.definition: a school for grownups, after all the other schools
very, very bad on purpose

spreads.title: The brewing
spreads.text:
Then she opened her book to the heaviest page,
and she lifted her wand, and she read, deep and slow,
and the cauldron leaned hungry, and greener, and wide —
and out of Moon, gently, like steam out of bread,
came the fire. The water. The gold-turning thread.
The growing. The mending. The swimming-like-silver.
And out of her sister, the same, every shine,
all swirling away in a long silver line,

down into the cauldron. And there, in the pot,
the powers went black. They went thick. They went ink.

(All but the one that she couldn't brew out,
the one that was never inside Moon at all.
It lives in other people. You remember.
Even a cauldron can't reach everyone.)

No almost. No rescue. No trick up a sleeve.
The witch won. She properly won.
The ink settled, thick, in the pot, like a night.
And Elysian nodded, and warmed up her thumb.
spreads.imagePrompt: The witch winning, seen wide in the green-lit cave: long ribbons of gold, silver, rose-pink and flame-red light streaming gently out of Moon and the small winged puppy, arcing bright through the dark and pouring down into the cauldron, where the colors sink and turn to thick glossy black like ink; the ribbons of stolen light are the brightest thing in the scene and light the witch's calm face from below, the skull-shape plain in her hair; Moon and the puppy sag, held upright by the pink-haired jaguar cub. Moon appears exactly once and the puppy appears exactly once — no duplicate characters. The scene is entirely inside the closed cave: no moon, no sky, no openings anywhere. Dramatic, flowing, sorrowful — never gory.

vocab.definition: spinning round and round, like water going down a drain

spreads.title: One line
spreads.text:
She dipped in her thumb, to the knuckle. She lifted
it, dripping with black that was blacker than black.
She was gentle. That's true. She was terribly gentle.
She painted one line on the pup. Just one line.

"There," said the witch, in her voice from the cellar.
"Finished. Now nothing can ever go wrong for her.
Nothing can ever go anything for her."

And Baby Lady opened her eyes. And they'd changed.
Not scary. Just flat. Like a pond with no wind in it.
And Moon reached out for her paw, like always —
three books of always —

and her sister looked at Moon's hand, and said, cold:
"You can stop looking at me now. I'm finished.
Finished things don't need sisters."

And of everything down in the dark of that cave —
the cauldron, the grin made of hair, all of it —
that was the worst thing.
That.
spreads.imagePrompt: Quiet, terrible, tender moment in the green-lit cave: the ancient witch bending gently down with one thumb extended, painting a single thin black line on the brow of the small winged puppy, who sits perfectly still and calm; Moon one step away with her hand stopped mid-reach, her face beginning to break; the puppy's round eyes gone flat and glassy-calm like a windless pond. Soft green light with bone-white accents; sad, hushed, never gory, no wounds, nothing physical wrong with the puppy.

vocab.definition: one of the bendy bumps in the middle of your fingers

spreads.title: Nothing to brew
spreads.text:
Then she turned to the jaguars, and readied her wand,
and read the page slower, to get it just right,
and the cauldron leaned hungry, and pulled at them, pulled —

and nothing came out.

For down in a cave there's no sea and no sky:
no water for her, and no weather for him.
And you can't brew a shine out of somebody shineless.
You can't pour a power from claws or a nose.
The spell slid right off them, like rain off a sail.

Well — one thing she found. In the cat. One small light,
grown out on the tip of one ordinary claw.
She pulled at it. Pulled. But a grown thing holds on.
It grew there, like whiskers. You can't pour a claw.

"Impossible," said the witch, slow, in the green.
"Everyone has something to take."
"Not us," said Cottontail, dry as the moon.
And Winds, in the dark, started smiling.
spreads.imagePrompt: In the green-lit cave: the witch aiming her thin black wand at the two young jaguar cubs as visible ripples of green spell-light wash over them and slide off like rain off a sail, taking nothing; the pink-haired cub stands planted and calm, one tiny warm gold spark glowing stubbornly on the tip of one small claw; beside her the grey-blue sky jaguar is beginning to grin, nose tilting up toward the dark ceiling. Green and black scene with three warm notes: the gold spark, pink hair, blue hair. Defiant, calm, not frightening.

vocab.definition: having no shine at all — none, not even a little
something that just can't happen (or so people say)

spreads.title: The hugest sniff
spreads.text:
Now a cave is a box with the lid shut down tight.
No sea for a sailor. No sky. And no weather.
But Winds stood stone-still in the blackest of black,
and his nose gave a twitch. Then a bigger one. Then —

his hugest sniff ever. And Winds started laughing.

"AIR!" hollered Winds, and it rang round the walls.
"MOVING air! I can smell it! The night! The outside!
The weather! It's THERE!" And he pointed his nose
at the roof of the deep, where nobody looks.

For you can bury that jaguar. Blindfold him. Spin him.
Wherever the out is, the out is deep in him.
And high in the roof was a crack, thin as eyelash,
where one drop of rain, every year, had been knocking —
politely, forever — and no one had heard.
spreads.imagePrompt: In the deepest black corner of the cave, away from the green glow: the grey-blue sky jaguar standing stone-still with his eyes closed and chin lifted in an enormous joyful sniff, grinning; one thin thread of silver moonlit air, the only silver in the whole scene, curling down from a hairline crack far up in the dark cave roof, with a single falling water drop catching the light; the pink-haired cub beside him following his gaze upward. The green cauldron-glow faint in the far background keeps the scene readable. Hope arriving as one thin silver line.

vocab.definition: in a kind, good-manners way
the very biggest of all

spreads.title: The roof opens
spreads.text:
Cottontail climbed. It's the thing that she does.
Wet stone, straight up, in the dark, just because
claws are not magic. Claws are just claws.
(You've heard that before. It was true then. It was.)

She reached the thin crack, and she hooked it, and pulled,
with Winds calling up through the dark, "TO YOUR LEFT!"
and the crack became wider. And wider. And then —

the roof of the cave opened up like a window.

And in came the night. The plain, ordinary night.
Plain rain. And plain moonlight. Plain silver-blue air.
The moon leaned in over the hole for a look —
the moon with its faint little line, from before —
and down came the rain into eighty years' dark,
and the cave, for the first time in anyone's ever,
had weather.

And here is a thing that the witch never learned,
for it isn't in spell books. It's plainer than they are:
ink is just ink.
And rain washes ink.
spreads.imagePrompt: The rescue, looking up: high on the wet black cave wall the pink-haired jaguar cub clings by her claws beside a crack she has pulled wide, and the cave roof stands open like a window to the night — deep indigo sky pouring through, sheets of plain silver rain falling all the way down into the dark, and a perfectly round full moon (never a crescent, bearing the faintest thin healed line) looking in through the opening; below, the sick green glow drowning under honest silver-blue light as small figures lift their faces to the rain. The ordinary night flooding back in like rescue.

vocab.definition: what the sky is doing — rain, wind, sun, or snow

spreads.title: The argument
spreads.text:
The rain found the pup where she stood, flat and quiet,
and washed at the one little line on her brow,
and the ink let go, and slid off like a shadow,
and her eyes filled back up, like a pool when the tide comes in.

And the very first thing that she did — the first thing —
was argue with Moon. About nothing. About RAIN.
"You're dripping on me," she said. "Move your wing over."
"It's raining on EVERYONE, Baby Lady."
"Well, your rain," she said, "is the drippiest rain."

And they argued! They argued! Their first one! Their EVER!
Three books full of never — and there, in the wet,
Moon laughed so hard that she cried, and the crying
got mixed with the rain till nobody could tell,
and she hugged her wet sister, who grumbled, "You're SOAKING,"
and hugged her right back, and grumbled some more.

And that dumb little argument, there in the rain,
was the happiest thing in this book. It just was.
spreads.imagePrompt: Joy in the silver rain inside the opened cave, warm gold and indigo flooding back over the fading green: the small winged puppy, soaked and bright-eyed again, mid-argument with Moon — both of them grinning through it — Moon's golden wing held over the puppy while rain streams off it, the last grey trickle of ink washing off the puppy's brow; around them the pink-haired cub, the blue-haired sky jaguar and the three pale sisters laugh in the downpour. Wet fur, wet hair, shining puddles, pure relief and happiness.

vocab.definition: the most drippy — dripping more than anything else

spreads.title: The rain she wouldn't stand in
spreads.text:
Then Moon — being Moon — turned around to the witch,
who stood at the edge of the silver, in shadow,
just out of the reach of the rain. And Moon said:
"It's only plain water. It isn't a magic.
It washes things off. Even old things. Even
eighty-year things.
You could stand in it too."

And Elysian looked at the rain a long time.
And the grin in her hair held terribly still.

Here is why she said no. (I'll say this part softly.)
If she stood in the rain, and the wrong washed away,
then the wrong was just wrong. A mix-up. A spill.
Two jars on a shelf, and a hand in a hurry.
Not a finishing. Never a finishing. Only
a thing that went wrong for a girl at a basin —
and eighty years out is a long way to walk back.

"I am finished," she said, in her voice like the deep.
And she gathered her wand and her book and her broom,
and she stepped from the silver and into the black,
where the rain hadn't reached, and would probably never,
and the dark of that cave goes a long, long way down,
and she knows every step.

Not beaten. Not sorry. Not fixed. And not done.
Gone deeper.
That's all.
Like a storm. Or a sun.
spreads.imagePrompt: At the boundary between silver rain-light and old black dark: Moon, small and gentle, holds one open hand out into the falling rain toward the ancient witch, who stands just beyond the rain's reach with her broom and wand and great book gathered in her arms, half turned away toward the deep of the cave; the skull-shape in her long hair holding perfectly still; behind her the cave floor slopes down into layer after layer of deeper dark. Rain-silver on one side, black on the other, one thin bright line between them. Dignified, sad, quiet; never gory.

vocab.definition: when two things get swapped by accident
all done, with nothing left to add or fix

spreads.title: The gift
spreads.text:
It rained all that night on the castle as well,
and the grownups came out and stood still in the pour,
and the quiet washed off them like ink. (It was ink.)
By breakfast the cook was out shooing the seagulls,
the guards were both grumping at mud on the stair,
and nobody ever, in any book ever,
was gladder to hear it. So there.

And that night, at the table (there's always a table;
there's always the soup, going round, going round),
Moon stood on her chair, with her sister beside her,
and they gave — to the jaguars — a gift. A forever one:
a great deal of power. To keep. Theirs. For good.
Not borrowed, like once on the deep dark sea —
given. On purpose. Freely. Out loud.

And it settled right into them. Settled, and stayed.
For a thing that is given sits deeper than poured,
and besides — in the cat, there was already a shine,
a small one, a grown one, her own, like a root,
and the gift wrapped around it and held.

And Winds stared down at his glowing paws.
"For ME?" said the wind-cat. "But all I did was SMELL!"
And Cottontail shrugged, with her spoon in her soup:
"Of course they did. Obviously.
That's what they're like."
spreads.imagePrompt: Cozy warm castle interior at night: the round wooden table crowded with steaming soup bowls under golden lamplight; Moon standing on her chair with the small winged puppy hovering beside her, the two of them pouring gentle streams of gold, silver and rose light down into the two young jaguar cubs — the grey-blue sky jaguar staring at his own faintly glowing front paws in open-mouthed astonishment, the pink-haired cub calmly mid-shrug with a spoon in her soup; around the table the three pale sisters, the girl in black writing in her small black book; and one extra empty chair with a full steaming bowl waiting in front of it. Crescent moon carved above the door; through the window a small perfectly round full moon in the sky (never a crescent). Every character is a small child. Warm, crowded, golden, safe.

vocab.definition: so easy to see that you don't even need to ask

spreads.title: The bowl
spreads.text:
And the bowl?

You remember the bowl. By the chair. Set each evening,
kept full for the stormy one, steam going up,
untouched every night since the end of the summer,
through autumn, through witch-times, through everything. Well.

Next morning the chair was pushed back. Just a little.
The spoon had been moved. And the bowl —

the bowl had been drunk from.

Nobody saw her. No door made a sound.
No wet mask, no grey cloak, no storm hanging round.
The window was latched and the lamps were all out.
But somebody came, in the quiet, alone,
and sat at the table, and drank the warm soup,
and left before morning could catch her.

And nobody said very much at all.
What is there to say? You already know.

They washed it.
They filled it.
They set it back down.
spreads.theEnd: The End — of the fourth one.
spreads.imagePrompt: Very quiet dawn interior, no characters anywhere: the round wooden table in pale early silver-gold light, chairs all tucked in except one pushed back a little; in front of that chair, a soup bowl clearly drunk from — half empty, spoon resting moved beside it — with the faintest last curl of steam; a few small drying rain-drops on the stone floor near the chair; the window latched, the lamps out, and through the window the perfectly round full moon (never a crescent, with the faintest thin healed line) setting pale over the sea. Crescent moon carved above the door. Stillness, tenderness, gentle mystery.

vocab.definition: left alone — nobody touched it at all
